sections.heading: Title
sections.text: What if a robot were told what to do by analogy, not by an exact goal image? This ICML 2022 work from Berkeley and Meta introduces goal-conditioned bisimulation: an abstraction where behaviorally equivalent state-goal pairs share a representation, so goals compose by arithmetic.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.text: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning usually hands the agent the exact goal, as a target image. But in the real world you rarely know the precise goal in advance. Ask a robot to close a drawer, and you may not know how the closed drawer looks. We want to specify tasks by analogy.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.text: Consider dicing a carrot versus a radish. The objects differ, but the skill and the change from start to goal are the same. Good representations are invariant to irrelevant details and equivariant to what varies. Prior bisimulation handled distractors for one task; we lift it to families of tasks.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text: The paper makes three contributions. It defines goal-conditioned bisimulation, grouping state-goal pairs that behave equivalently. It gives a metric-learning objective so new goals arise from latent arithmetic. And it proves the representation is sufficient for any state-only reward task.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: GCB learns two encoders together. Phi encodes a state-goal pair so its L1 distance matches an on-policy bisimulation metric, capturing how differently two tasks behave. Psi encodes a state so the goal embedding minus the state embedding equals phi. That makes goals composable: add an analogous pair to your state, then take the nearest neighbor in psi space. Training is offline on Implicit Q-Learning.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.text: GCB is tested in a PyBullet manipulation suite of random workspaces built from eighty-four object geometries. Tasks span Drawer, Button-and-Drawer, and Analogy, each also run with added video distractors to probe robustness. Results average over five seeds.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.text: Across six settings, GCB is top on five, and wins on every distractor task. It reaches about forty-five percent on Drawer with distractors and thirty-two on Button-and-Drawer. On analogy tasks, where the goal is inferred from an example, it roughly doubles the next-best baseline.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.text: Ablations confirm the design. Adding a grounding term, phi of a goal with itself, as a normalizing constant in psi's objective helps. An L1 metric loss for phi beats L2. And varying the latent dimensionality barely changes control.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.text: Some headline numbers. On Drawer with video distractors, GCB reaches zero point four four eight, best of any method. On Button-and-Drawer with distractors, zero point three two two. On analogy, zero point four zero three versus zero point one seven six for the next best.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.text: The takeaway: treating bisimulation as an equivalence over tasks, not just states, aligns analogous tasks in one space. Because goals become composable by arithmetic, you can point a robot at an example and have it infer its own goal, provably sufficient for any state-only reward task.
